---
title: "Telling touching nuclei apart"
description: "One dataset read two ways, and why the decoding is part of the number."
mirrors: instances
---

`data_science_bowl.yaml` finds the nuclei in these pictures and stops there. The mask it
produces says *nucleus* or *not nucleus* for every pixel, so two nuclei touching each other
come back as one region, and **a count taken from it would be wrong**.

This is the same dataset, read a different way. Nothing new was collected: the 2018 Data
Science Bowl ships one mask per nucleus, and `data_science_bowl.yaml` unites them. Here they
keep their identity, which turns the question from *where are the nuclei* into *how many are
there, and which pixels belong to which one*.

**Where the numbers come from.** The two object counts below, and every shape figure in
*What shape, which needs no scale at all*, were produced by running the code shown, on this
machine, against the published weights - no training. They are **one run** rather than a
property of the task: inference on fixed weights is near enough deterministic that the
counts should reproduce, and the last digit of a median over 5,378 objects is not something
this page asks anybody to match. Everything else is cited where it is used: the weights'
three scores are the registry's own description, the ceilings are `pyplatypus#159` and
`#212`, and the trained rows are
`examples/publish_dsbowl_instance_weights.py`'s. That division is deliberate - an article
that re-trains a published recipe with fewer epochs adds a number nobody will compare.

## Before any of that: objects in four lines

Weights for this are published, so the difference is visible before anything is trained.
The borrowed model predicts three channels - background, the interior of a nucleus and a rim
around it - and `decode` says how those channels become objects:

```python
import pyplatypus as pp

borrowed = pp.from_dict(
    {
        "task": "instance_segmentation",
        "data": {
            "train_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "validation_path": "examples/data/data_science_bowl/stage1_validation",
            "mode": "nested_dirs",
        },
        "models": [
            {
                "name": "published",
                "architecture": "u_net",
                "input_shape": [256, 256],
                "blocks": 4,
                "filters": 16,
                "separation": {"name": "rim", "width": 2},
                "decode": [{"name": "nearest_seed"}, {"name": "connected_components"}],
                "weights": "dsbowl-instances",
                "fit": False,
            }
        ],
    }
)
engine = pp.build_engine(borrowed)
engine.fit()
objects = engine.predict_instances(split="validation", decode="nearest_seed")
len(objects)
```

**`fit()` is still the call, and `fit: false` only changes what it does.** With the flag set
it loads rather than trains, and nothing before it has touched the weights: `build_engine`
reads the data and builds the model, so a `predict` straight after it is refused with *no
model has been trained or loaded yet*. That is one line a reader would otherwise find out
by being refused, and this page had it wrong in its first version.

Loading does check the weights against the model they are going into, and before torch is
reached: a wrong shape is a refusal naming the field rather than a tensor-size error from
inside a loss.

`predict_instances` returns **one integer label map per image, in the split's own order** -
objects numbered from 1, with 0 for background. A list rather than a stacked array, because
what a caller does with these is read one case at a time.

`predict` is the other call and it is not the same thing: it returns the model's own
channels, class probabilities and raw vector components, which is what `predict_instances`
decodes. A softmax across a flow component and a class would return a number and mean
nothing, so that one is left raw.

Now the same loaded file, decoded the other way. `connected_components` ignores the rim
channel entirely - it labels connected foreground, which is what a semantic mask gives you:

```python
merged = engine.predict_instances(split="validation", decode="connected_components")

counts = [(a.max(), b.max()) for a, b in zip(objects, merged)]
worst = max(range(len(counts)), key=lambda i: counts[i][0] - counts[i][1])
counts[worst]
```

On the picture where the two disagree most, that is **245 objects against 180**: one file of
weights, one forward pass, two answers to *how many nuclei are in this picture*, and
sixty-five touching nuclei run together by the second. Over all 134 images it is **5,378
against 4,914**, which is the same gap counted once rather than per picture. Drawn with `overlay_instances`,
neither colour map is decoration - adjacent objects are guaranteed different colours, so a
colour shared across a boundary is two nuclei the decoding ran together.

**No score is reported here, on purpose.** These weights were trained on `stage1_train` and
this directory is `stage1_validation`, which is the split they were measured on - the numbers
that mean something travel with them, and `available_weights()` carries them:

```
U-Net, 256x256, nuclei in light microscopy, trained to separate touching objects:
interior, rim and background. BBBC038v1 (the 2018 Data Science Bowl, CC0), the same 134
held-out images as `dsbowl-unet`. **One file, three scores** - instance average
precision 0.5445 by nearest_seed, 0.5390 by watershed and 0.4822 by
connected_components - so a number from these weights means nothing without the
decoding it came from. Foreground Dice 0.9118. The separation signal is worth +0.0623
here while a perfect mask is worth +0.2398: the mask is the limit on this data, not the
signal.
```

That description is the thing to read before quoting anything. **One file, three scores**:
the decoding is part of the number, and 0.0623 separates the best from the worst.

## The semantic sibling, side by side

`dsbowl-unet` is the published model `data_science_bowl.yaml` trains: same data, same
held-out images, one foreground class. It is the comparison this whole document is about, so
it is worth running rather than describing - the same `from_dict` with
`task: semantic_segmentation`, a `colormap` of black and white, and
`weights: dsbowl-unet`. Its `predict` returns a stacked array of masks, not a list of label
maps, and that difference is the whole point.

A mask is not worse. It answers a different question, and if the answer you need is *what
fraction of this slide is nuclei* it is the one to use. The label map is what you need to
count them, or to measure one of them.

## The data

The directory layout is `data_science_bowl.yaml`'s, because it is the same directory:

```
stage1_train/
  00ae65c1c.../
    images/00ae65c1c....png
    masks/8a0ac8e3c....png      # one file per nucleus, 70 of them in this case
    masks/9a1e2f4b7....png
    ...
```

536 cases in `stage1_train`, and `mode: nested_dirs` is what reads that shape. The one
difference from the semantic file is the task: `instance_segmentation` reads those
per-object files as identities, where `semantic_segmentation` takes their element-wise
maximum and destroys them.

## The specification, with the borrowed model beside a new one

Two models in one file, and `evaluate()` returns a row per model **and decoding**, so one
table holds the comparison the rest of this document rests on. The shipped version of this
is `examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml`, which trains `rim` beside `flows` rather
than a borrowed file beside a new one - two separation signals, which is the question that
file was written to answer.

`separation` is one block per model and `decode` is a list, and the asymmetry is not
cosmetic: the separation sets what the network predicts, so changing it means another
training run, while a second decoding is another pass over the same predictions. Measured on
these 134 images, a second decoding costs **1.41 seconds** against sixteen minutes for a
second training run - so the right analogy is `metrics:` and not `callbacks:`.

`connected_components` is in both models' `decode` lists on purpose. It ignores the
separation signal, so it is the row the other rows have to be read against: not a weaker
model, the same model asked a question that throws half its output away.

## Train

```python
spec = pp.from_yaml("examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml")
engine = pp.build_engine(spec, num_workers=4)
history = engine.fit(verbose=True)
```

`num_workers=4` is worth copying: the GPU spends most of a run waiting for PNGs to be
decoded, and nothing about the model changes.

The epoch counts in that file are asymmetric and deliberately so - 120 for `rim` against 60
for `flows`. Measured at 60 each on 2026-10-13, `rim` was still climbing while `flows` had
flattened, and a table ranking two models needs both converged or a column reports the
budget rather than the signal.

## Compare

`engine.evaluate("validation")` returns one row per *(model, decoding)*. Three things in it,
in the order they matter.

**Within either model, the mask is identical across its rows.** There is one forward pass;
the rows differ only in how its channels were turned into objects. So the spread between a
model's own rows is the decoding's contribution and nothing else.

**`connected_components` is the row the others are read against**, for the reason above.

**The two separation signals are a tie.** `rim` is worth +0.0676 of instance average
precision over its own `connected_components` row and `flows` +0.0661 - a difference of
0.0015 against a run-to-run spread of **0.0112** measured on that same file. On foreground
Dice they are 0.9159 and 0.9097, which is 0.0062 apart.

That last number is worth a warning, because the table had it wrong once. `dice` is a mean
over whichever class channels a head has - three for `rim`, two for `flows` - so the column
named `dice` compares two different quantities and showed the two masks 0.09 apart **with
the sign reversed**. `foreground_dice` is the one to read across models; `class dice` is the
honest name for the other.

## What this does not settle, measured rather than guessed

The instance milestone closed on numbers that say the interesting part is somewhere else:

| route | instance AP on these 134 images |
|---|---|
| the published semantic weights through connected components | 0.4888 |
| **a perfect semantic mask** through connected components | **0.7655** |
| the published separation weights, `nearest_seed` | 0.5445 |
| a perfect mask through the same separation route | 0.9846 |

So connected components caps *any* model here at 0.7655 - a flawless mask still scores that
- and the separation signal is worth about +0.06 on top of the mask it is computed from,
where fixing the mask is worth +0.24. Three trained signals were compared and they agree.

Read that as a closed direction rather than as a run to tune: on this data the headroom is
in the mask, and a document that ended on a score would be claiming the opposite of what was
measured.

## Which objects, not how many pixels

A score cannot tell you whether you found the wrong nuclei or drew the right ones badly.
`overlay_instance_agreement` matches predicted objects to true ones the way the metric does
and colours the three outcomes, so the failure is visible by kind: a true object a
prediction matched, one that nothing matched, and a prediction matching nothing.

The truth has to be assembled from the per-object files, and `read_image(nearest=True)`
matters - interpolating a label map invents numbers belonging to no object:

```python
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

def truth_map(case: Path, size=(256, 256)) -> np.ndarray:
    labels = np.zeros(size, dtype=np.int32)
    for index, file in enumerate(sorted((case / "masks").glob("*.png")), start=1):
        mask = pp.read_image(file, channels=1, size=size, nearest=True)
        labels[mask[..., 0] > 0.5] = index
    return labels
```

The threshold the matching uses is an IoU of 0.5 and it cannot be lowered below that: under
0.5 one prediction can satisfy two true objects at once, the match stops being one to one,
and the average precision refuses the same thing for the same reason.

## A decoding changed without retraining

This is what `decode` being a list is for. No model is loaded again and nothing is trained:

```python
for how in ("nearest_seed", "watershed", "connected_components"):
    maps = engine.predict_instances("rim", split="validation", decode=how)
    print(how, sum(int(m.max()) for m in maps))
```

Against 5,999 objects in the truth over 134 images. The counts, not the scores, are where
the decoding shows itself most plainly: the gap between the first row and the last is nuclei
that were found and then run together with a neighbour.

## What it was for: a count and a size distribution

One label map in, one row per object out, and `instance_sizes()` is that row:

```python
labels = engine.predict_instances("rim", split="validation", decode="nearest_seed")[0]
rows = pp.instance_sizes(labels)
```

**This paragraph said the opposite for two days and the correction is worth more than the
sentence.** It read *"this is the one place where the R package has a function and this one
deliberately does not"*, argued that `numpy.unique` with `return_counts` *is* the operation
so a wrapper would be a name to learn, and pointed a reader at the R package instead. That
was true when it was written on 2026-10-23 and false on 2026-10-25, when `0.8.0a39` put
`mask_volume()`, `instance_sizes()` and three more into `pyplatypus.measure` - because every
route from a mask to a physical unit was reachable from R and from nowhere else, which is the
same defect this paragraph was describing as a decision.

**And the instrument had been taught to look away from exactly this name.**
`tests/test_articles.py` resolves a backticked name followed by parentheses against this
package, and the old text wrote `instance_sizes` *without* them on purpose, with a paragraph
explaining that a name belonging to the other package is named rather than offered. The
reasoning was right and it bought a blind spot: the one name whose claim could go stale was
the one name the test could not see. It carries parentheses now, so the test holds it.

**In pixels, because this dataset has no physical scale.** A CT scan carries its spacing in
its header and `target_spacing` is where that enters a run; these are microscopy images with
no calibration recorded, so a number in micrometres here would be invented. A count is still
a count.

### What shape, which needs no scale at all

`instance_shapes()` answers the other half - not how big an object is but how stretched -
and it is the one measurement this uncalibrated dataset can report honestly, because
`eccentricity` is a **ratio**. One row per object, out of one pass over the label map:

```python
shapes = pp.instance_shapes(labels)
```

Measured on all 134 validation images through the published weights, 5,378 objects:

    eccentricity   median 0.7422   q10 0.4396   q90 0.9097   12.09% above 0.9
    semi-axes      major 7.68 px   minor 4.85 px, both medians
    axis ratio     median 0.6580

So a nucleus here is typically half again as long as it is wide, and an eighth of them are
strongly elongated. **125 of the 5,378 have no shape at all** - fewer than three pixels is no
second moment - and they come back as zeros rather than as an error, which is the right
answer for a speck and would be the wrong answer to hide.

**"Needs no scale" is true because the pixels are square, and that is measured rather than
assumed.** `eccentricity` is unitless and it is *not* spacing-free: it describes whichever
space it was computed in. On the busiest of these images, the same 245 objects:

    no spacing, the grid        median eccentricity 0.7622
    spacing (0.5, 0.5)          median eccentricity 0.7622
    spacing (1.0, 0.5)          median eccentricity 0.9169

An isotropic spacing changes nothing and an anisotropic one moves the median by 0.15, so the
grid's answer is the object's answer **only** while a pixel is as tall as it is wide. That is
what the `_px` suffix on the axes is for: with a spacing the columns are `major_mm` and
`minor_mm`, without one they are `major_px` and `minor_px`, and the suffix on the neighbours
is what says which space the row is in.

A volume gets three axes and no eccentricity, since an ellipsoid has no single one.

## The same thing from a file

Everything above is one file in this repository:

```python
spec = pp.from_yaml("examples/data_science_bowl_instances.yaml")
```

That file is also the longest commented configuration here, because two of its decisions
needed their reasons written down: the asymmetric epoch counts, and a correction kept in
place rather than deleted after `dice` was read across two models with different numbers of
class channels. The configuration guide's *Instances instead of one mask* section has the
same fields with a reader's explanation beside each.

## A note on older graphics cards

PyTorch 2.8 and later ship CUDA 13 builds, and CUDA 13 dropped the Maxwell, Pascal and Volta
generations - a GTX 10-series card cannot run them, and no driver update changes that.

This package does not install torch and will not choose a build for you, which is the
difference from the R package: there, `platypus_use_torch("pascal")` exists because
`reticulate` provisions the environment and something has to decide. Here you install your
own, so the equivalent is asking your index for the CUDA 12 wheels before anything else. If
`torch.cuda.is_available()` is `False` on a machine that has a GPU, that is the first thing
to check - otherwise everything above runs on the processor instead, perhaps ten times
slower, and says nothing about it.
